entries.map_query: Washington Square Park New York
entries.excerpt: So he walked with her through the devious ways of the west side of the town, and through the bustle of gathering nightfall in populous streets, to the quiet precinct of Washington Square. They lingered a moment at the foot of Dr. Sloper’s white marble steps, above which a spotless white door, adorned with a glittering silver plate, seemed to figure, for Morris, the closed portal of happiness; and then Mrs. Penniman’s companion rested a melancholy eye upon a lighted window in the upper part of the house.
entries.note: James moves from the crowded streets into a quiet square. The white door of the fictional Sloper house becomes a boundary between Morris Townsend and the life he hopes to enter.
entries.precision: Area described. The pin marks the square, not an identified address for the fictional house.
entries.visit_note: Explore the square and its north-side streets from public paths.

entries.map_query: Metropolitan Museum of Art New York
entries.excerpt: Avoiding the popular "Wolfe collection," whose anecdotic canvases filled one of the main galleries of the queer wilderness of cast-iron and encaustic tiles known as the Metropolitan Museum, they had wandered down a passage to the room where the "Cesnola antiquities" mouldered in unvisited loneliness.
entries.note: Archer and Ellen find privacy among antiquities. Wharton makes the museum feel secluded and faintly melancholy, a refuge from the social scrutiny outside.
entries.precision: Named institution. The historical gallery arrangement in the novel is not a guide to the museum today.
entries.visit_note: The museum is at 1000 Fifth Avenue. Check admission and opening hours before visiting.

entries.map_query: Ed Koch Queensboro Bridge New York
entries.excerpt: Over the great bridge, with the sunlight through the girders making a constant flicker upon the moving cars, with the city rising up across the river in white heaps and sugar lumps all built with a wish out of nonolfactory money. The city seen from the Queensboro Bridge is always the city seen for the first time, in its first wild promise of all the mystery and the beauty in the world.
entries.note: Nick approaches Manhattan with Gatsby. The bridge turns the familiar skyline into a promise of reinvention, just as Gatsby is presenting his own story.
entries.precision: Named bridge. The pin identifies the crossing, not a precise viewpoint or pedestrian entrance.
entries.visit_note: Use Google Maps for a current pedestrian approach; the passage describes a journey by car.

entries.map_query: Central Park South New York

entries.excerpt: When Jordan Baker had finished telling all this we had left the Plaza for half an hour and were driving in a victoria through Central Park. The sun had gone down behind the tall apartments of the movie stars in the West Fifties, and the clear voices of children, already gathered like crickets on the grass, rose through the hot twilight:
entries.excerpt_kind: Paragraph leading into a quoted song

entries.map_query: The Battery New York
entries.excerpt: There now is your insular city of the Manhattoes, belted round by wharves as Indian isles by coral reefs—commerce surrounds it with her surf. Right and left, the streets take you waterward. Its extreme downtown is the battery, where that noble mole is washed by waves, and cooled by breezes, which a few hours previous were out of sight of land. Look at the crowds of water-gazers there.
entries.note: Before Ishmael goes to sea, he watches New Yorkers drawn to the waterfront. The Battery becomes the city’s threshold to an ocean that seems to pull people out of their everyday lives.
entries.precision: Area described. The pin is on the present-day waterfront; the shoreline has changed since Melville wrote.
entries.visit_note: Follow the public waterfront paths; this is not a reconstructed nineteenth-century viewpoint.

entries.map_query: Madison Square Park New York
entries.locator: “The Cop and the Anthem,” opening paragraph
entries.excerpt: On his bench in Madison Square Soapy moved uneasily. When wild geese honk high of nights, and when women without sealskin coats grow kind to their husbands, and when Soapy moves uneasily on his bench in the park, you may know that winter is near at hand.
entries.note: The park bench is Soapy’s home, and the first signs of winter are an urgent problem. O. Henry measures the changing season from the perspective of someone who has nowhere warm to go.
entries.precision: Named park. Soapy’s bench is fictional and has no identified present-day location.
entries.visit_note: Visit the public park between Fifth Avenue, Madison Avenue, 23rd and 26th Streets.

entries.map_query: Fulton Ferry Landing Brooklyn New York
entries.locator: “Crossing Brooklyn Ferry,” section 1; later collected text
entries.excerpt:
Flood-tide below me! I see you face to face!
Clouds of the west—sun there half an hour high—I see you also face to face.
Crowds of men and women attired in the usual costumes, how curious you are to me!
On the ferry-boats the hundreds and hundreds that cross, returning home, are more curious to me than you suppose,
And you that shall cross from shore to shore years hence are more to me, and more in my meditations, than you might suppose.
entries.note: Whitman looks at commuters on the river and addresses people who will cross it long after him. The shared view becomes a connection between strangers across generations.
entries.precision: Historical crossing. The pin marks the Brooklyn landing associated with the Fulton Ferry, not the poet’s exact position.
entries.visit_note: Read from the public waterfront. The old crossing and today’s ferry services are different.

entries.map_query: Lenox Avenue Harlem New York
entries.excerpt: Turning out of the park into the broad thoroughfare of Lenox Avenue, Mrs. Hayes-Rore said in a too carefully casual manner: “And, by the way, I wouldn’t mention that my people are white, if I were you. Colored people won’t understand it, and after all it’s your own business. When you’ve lived as long as I have, you’ll know that what others don’t know can’t hurt you. I’ll just tell Anne that you’re a friend of mine whose mother’s dead. That’ll place you well enough and it’s all true. I never tell lies. She can fill in the gaps to suit herself and anyone else curious enough to ask.”
entries.note: Entering Harlem, Helga receives advice about concealing her white family. The avenue is a threshold into a community whose welcome carries its own rules.

entries.map_query: Harlem New York
entries.excerpt: A year thick with various adventures had sped by since that spring day on which Helga Crane had set out away from Chicago’s indifferent unkindness for New York in the company of Mrs. Hayes-Rore. New York she had found not so unkind, not so unfriendly, not so indifferent. There she had been happy, and secured work, had made acquaintances and another friend. Again she had had that strange transforming experience, this time not so fleetingly, that magic sense of having come home. Harlem, teeming black Harlem, had welcomed her and lulled her into something that was, she was certain, peace and contentment.
entries.note: Helga initially experiences Harlem as an arrival home. Larsen makes the neighborhood a place of work, friendship and provisional peace.
entries.precision: Neighborhood described, not a particular house or venue.

entries.map_query: Saint Nicholas Park Manhattan New York
entries.excerpt: Always her forehead wrinkled in distaste whenever, involuntarily, which was somehow frequently, her mind turned on the speculative gray eyes and visionary uplifting plans of Dr. Anderson. That other, James Vayle, had slipped absolutely from her consciousness. Of him she never thought. Helga Crane meant, now, to have a home and perhaps laughing, appealing dark-eyed children in Harlem. Her existence was bounded by Central Park, Fifth Avenue, St. Nicholas Park, and One Hundred and Forty-fifth street. Not at all a narrow life, as Negroes live it, as Helga Crane knew it. Everything was there, vice and goodness, sadness and gayety, ignorance and wisdom, ugliness and beauty, poverty and richness. And it seemed to her that somehow of goodness, gayety, wisdom, and beauty always there was a little more than of vice, sadness, ignorance, and ugliness. It was only riches that did not quite transcend poverty.
entries.note: Helga names the edges of a world that seems to contain everything she needs. St. Nicholas Park appears as one boundary of that imagined completeness.
entries.precision: Named park used as a neighborhood boundary. This passage does not place Helga at a specific spot inside it.

entries.map_query: Coney Island Brooklyn New York
entries.excerpt: By reason of the fact that my living expenses in the South had been very small, I still had nearly four hundred dollars of my capital left. In contemplation of this, my natural and acquired Bohemian tastes asserted themselves, and I decided to have a couple of weeks’ good time before worrying seriously about the future. I went to Coney Island and the other resorts, took in the preseason shows along Broadway, and ate at first-class restaurants; but I shunned the old Sixth Avenue district as though it were pest-infected. My few days of pleasure made appalling inroads upon what cash I had, and caused me to see that it required a good deal of money to live in New York as I wished to live and that I should have to find, very soon, some more or less profitable employment. I was sure that unknown, without friends or prestige, it would be useless to try to establish myself as a teacher of music; so I gave that means of earning a livelihood scarcely any consideration. And even had I considered it possible to secure pupils, as I then felt, I should have hesitated about taking up a work in which the chances for any considerable financial success are necessarily so small. I had made up my mind that since I was not going to be a Negro, I would avail myself of every possible opportunity to make a white man’s success; and that, if it can be summed up in any one word, means “money.”
entries.note: Returning to New York, the narrator spends his savings on the city’s pleasures. Coney Island belongs to a brief holiday before his search for financial security.
entries.precision: Named resort district. The narrator identifies no particular attraction.

entries.map_query: Madison Avenue and East 45th Street New York
entries.excerpt: They turned into Madison Avenue and began to stroll northward. As she moved beside him, with her long light step, Selden was conscious of taking a luxurious pleasure in her nearness: in the modelling of her little ear, the crisp upward wave of her hair⁠—was it ever so slightly brightened by art?⁠—and the thick planting of her straight black lashes. Everything about her was at once vigorous and exquisite, at once strong and fine. He had a confused sense that she must have cost a great deal to make, that a great many dull and ugly people must, in some mysterious way, have been sacrificed to produce her. He was aware that the qualities distinguishing her from the herd of her sex were chiefly external: as though a fine glaze of beauty and fastidiousness had been applied to vulgar clay. Yet the analogy left him unsatisfied, for a coarse texture will not take a high finish; and was it not possible that the material was fine, but that circumstance had fashioned it into a futile shape?
entries.note: As Lily and Selden stroll north, his admiration turns into an inventory of the expense and labor behind her beauty. The avenue frames a gaze shaped by class.
entries.precision: Named avenue. The map marks a representative point near Grand Central, not a documented stopping place.

entries.map_query: Wall Street New York
entries.excerpt: Lily’s mind had reverted from the intrusive personality of Mr. Rosedale to the train of thought set in motion by Trenor’s first words. This vast mysterious Wall Street world of “tips” and “deals”⁠—might she not find in it the means of escape from her dreary predicament? She had often heard of women making money in this way through their friends: she had no more notion than most of her sex of the exact nature of the transaction, and its vagueness seemed to diminish its indelicacy. She could not, indeed, imagine herself, in any extremity, stooping to extract a “tip” from Mr. Rosedale; but at her side was a man in possession of that precious commodity, and who, as the husband of her dearest friend, stood to her in a relation of almost fraternal intimacy.
entries.note: For Lily, Wall Street is an obscure system that might rescue her finances. Its apparent distance from her social life disguises how closely the two worlds are tied.
entries.precision: Named financial district used as a metaphor for investing. Lily is thinking about Wall Street here, not walking along it.

entries.map_query: Bryant Park New York
entries.excerpt: Lily walked on unconscious of her surroundings. She was still treading the buoyant ether which emanates from the high moments of life. But gradually it shrank away from her and she felt the dull pavement beneath her feet. The sense of weariness returned with accumulated force, and for a moment she felt that she could walk no farther. She had reached the corner of Forty-first Street and Fifth Avenue, and she remembered that in Bryant Park there were seats where she might rest.
entries.note: Exhausted after leaving Selden, Lily remembers the park’s benches. A public resting place takes on a new importance when private security has slipped away.
entries.precision: Named park. The text identifies her approach at Forty-first Street and Fifth Avenue, but no exact bench.

entries.excerpt: Fifth and Sixth Avenues, it seemed to Anthony, were the uprights of a gigantic ladder stretching from Washington Square to Central Park. Coming uptown on top of a bus toward Fifty-Second Street invariably gave him the sensation of hoisting himself hand by hand on a series of treacherous rungs, and when the bus jolted to a stop at his own rung he found something akin to relief as he descended the reckless metal steps to the sidewalk.
entries.note: Anthony imagines Fifth and Sixth Avenues as a ladder. A routine bus ride turns the city’s grid into an anxious climb toward his apartment.

entries.map_query: Grand Street and Essex Street New York
entries.excerpt: ONE Friday evening in September I stood on Grand Street with my eyes raised to the big open windows of a dance-hall on the second floor of a brick building on the opposite side of the lively thoroughfare. Only the busts of the dancers could be seen. This and the distance that divided me from the hall enveloped the scene in mystery. As the couples floated by, as though borne along on waves of the music, the girls clinging to the men, their fantastic figures held me spellbound. Several other people were watching the dancers from the street, mostly women, who gazed at the appearing and disappearing images with envying eyes
entries.note: David watches dancers through second-floor windows. The distance between pavement and ballroom turns ordinary entertainment into a vision of a life he cannot yet enter.

entries.map_query: Canal Street and Orchard Street New York
entries.excerpt: I MADE it my business to visit a well-known Hebrew book-store on Canal Street. I asked for Tevkin's works. It appeared that before he emigrated to America he had published three small volumes of verse and prose, that they had once aroused much interest, but that they were now practically out of print. I tried two other stores, with the same result. I was referred to the Astor Library, whose Hebrew department was becoming one of the richest in the world. Sitting down in a public library to read a book seemed to be an undignified proceeding for a manufacturer to engage in, but my curiosity was beyond considerations of this sort. Whenever I thought of Miss Tevkin I beheld the image of those three books—the only things related to her with which I was able to come in contact
entries.note: A search for Tevkin’s books takes David from Hebrew bookshops toward the Astor Library. Literary curiosity momentarily disturbs his assumptions about a businessman’s dignity.
entries.precision: Named street with unidentified bookshops. The map marks Canal Street, not a claim that a particular store survives.

entries.map_query: Suffolk Street and Delancey Street New York
entries.excerpt: And so the “stoops,” sidewalks, and pavements of Suffolk Street were thronged with panting, chattering, or frisking multitudes. In one spot the scene received a kind of weird picturesqueness from children dancing on the pavement to the strident music hurled out into the tumultuous din from a row of the open and brightly illuminated windows of what appeared to be a new tenement house. Some of the young women on the sidewalk opposite raised a longing eye to these windows, for floating, by through the dazzling light within were young women like themselves with masculine arms round their waists.
entries.note: The street, stoops and dance hall share one crowded summer evening. Cahan moves between people watching from outside and couples turning in the bright windows above.
entries.precision: Named street. The fictional dancing academy is not assigned a real building number.

entries.map_query: Essex Street and Delancey Street New York
entries.locator: Chapter III, “In the Grip of His Past”
entries.excerpt: Jake had never even vaguely abandoned the idea of supplying his wife and child with the means of coming to join him. He was more or less prompt in remitting her monthly allowance of ten rubles, and the visit to the draft and passage office had become part of the routine of his life. It had the invariable effect of arousing his dormant scruples, and he hardly ever left the office without ascertaining the price of a steerage voyage from Hamburg to New York. But no sooner did he emerge from the dingy basement into the noisy scenes of Essex Street, than he would consciously let his mind wander off to other topics.
entries.note: The passage office briefly awakens Jake’s responsibility to his wife and child. Once he returns to noisy Essex Street, he deliberately lets it fade.
entries.precision: Named street. The remittance and ticket office is not given a verified street number.

entries.map_query: Delancey Street and Essex Street New York
